lesson.title: Falling Apart Alone: Unimolecular Reactions
lesson.summary: A unimolecular elementary step involves a single reactant particle rearranging or breaking apart on its own, giving first-order kinetics that come directly from its molecularity of one.
lesson.body:
A unimolecular reaction is an elementary step in which exactly one reactant particle undergoes the change, whether that means the molecule breaks apart into smaller fragments, or simply rearranges its own atoms into a different structural arrangement, without needing to collide with a second reactant particle to do it. This is the molecularity-1 case introduced in the Molecularity chapter: only one particle is involved in the step itself.

Common real examples include isomerization reactions, where a molecule flips from one structural arrangement to another without changing its molecular formula, such as cyclopropane rearranging into propene, and unimolecular decompositions, where a single molecule splits into two or more smaller product molecules or fragments, such as a single step in the breakdown of a strained or unstable molecule into simpler products.

Because a unimolecular step is elementary, you can write its rate law directly from its molecularity, exactly as you did for other elementary steps: with only one reactant particle involved, the rate law is first order in that reactant:

rate = k[A]

This is a case where the elementary-step shortcut and everyday intuition line up neatly: one molecule reacting on its own gives a rate law with an exponent of exactly one.

It is worth pausing on an interesting subtlety, since it is easy to get the wrong idea from the phrase "unimolecular." Even though only one molecule is involved in the actual bond-breaking or rearranging event, that molecule still needed to acquire enough energy to do it, and molecules mostly gain extra energy the same way they always do: by colliding with something else, often just an ordinary, unreactive molecule bumping into them and transferring energy. So a "unimolecular" reaction is not really happening in total isolation from collisions; it simply means that once a molecule has already been energized, the actual reactive event, the step chemists are describing when they call it unimolecular, involves that one molecule acting alone. The energizing collision and the unimolecular transformation are treated as two separate matters, and it is specifically the transformation step, not the energizing step, that gets the label unimolecular and the first-order rate law.
